narrative:
September opens with heat you'd find oppressive even in July. Sunshine rules today with a few afternoon clouds. I can't completely rule out a late-day thundershower. Wednesday and Thursday are the "peak of the heat" days with potential to break heat records for the dates in the Southern Appalachians. Wednesday has even lower afternoon thundershower potential than today, but Thursday afternoon has more. The weekend brings a transition to a break in the heat early next week.

The Monday Message is back today for our subscribers! We have a hot week, yielding to a cooler Labor Day holiday weekend.

Subscribe Forecast Discussion The September Sizzle comes from a strong ridge of high pressure parked over the Southeast. It peaks Wednesday. Skies stay mostly sunny today and Wednesday with a few afternoon clouds. A late-day thundershower can't be completely ruled out either day, but a warm layer aloft holds thunderstorm development mostly in check. Record highs will be in jeopardy both Wednesday and Thursday. Thursday, the ridge begins to fray along its northern edge. Afternoon clouds increase, and widely scattered showers and thunderstorms return while the heat holds near record levels. Friday, a cold front approaches from the north. Widely scattered afternoon thunderstorms again in play, a few lingering into early evening. The front crosses Saturday. Computer guidance leaves timing details as a point of uncertainty: widely scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms that may linger into the evening. Sunday is less warm behind the front, but it's not a mad rush to cooler. Showers and thunderstorms remain possible, especially in the afternoon. Labor Day is the coolest day of the stretch, as high pressure wedges down the east side of the Appalachians. Clouds are more prominent with scattered showers. Tuesday we begin a gradual temperature rebound. Tropical Storm Edouard makes landfall on the Texas/Louisiana coast today and dissipates over east Texas by Thursday, steered around the same ridge that's giving us the heat. No direct impacts here. Aug 31, 2026 September 2026 Forecast Outlook Forecast Monthly Forecast September 2026 Weather Outlook Southern Appalachians – SW Virginia & Western North Carolina September 2026 will open very warm, then trend gradually toward typical September weather as the month goes on. After two wet months, the pattern turns drier than average — with a tropical season held down by El Niño as the one wildcard. The lead graphic for this document shows expected overall monthly anomalies for both temperature (warmer) and precipitation (drier). The Typical September: Summertime Slipping Away Well, the sun's not so hot in the sky today
And you know I can see summertime slipping on away
A few more geese are gone, a few more leaves turning red
But the grass is as soft as a feather in a featherbed
— James Taylor, "September Grass" James Taylor has it right. September is the month the mountains change their mind about summer. August gives up almost nothing; September gives up a lot, and most of it in the second half. The average high falls nine to ten degrees between the first of the month and the last, and the nights lead the way, cooling faster than the days. The rain changes character more than amount. September is nearly as wet as August on average, but the afternoon thunderstorms that ruled the summer fade. The Foothills dry out more than the mountains — North Wilkesboro and Hickory average half an inch to an inch less rainfall than in August. The high peaks are different: Mt Mitchell, on average, is wetter in September than August. And this is the peak of hurricane season, when a single tropical remnant has produced some of the region's largest rain totals. A September tropical event in the area decides how the month is remembered. The Big Picture for September 2026 The month begins with the pattern August never delivered. A large ridge of high pressure aloft builds over the Southeast in the first days of September and holds through the first week. This will be the warmest stretch of the month. The ridge then slides slowly west, over Tennessee and Kentucky and on toward the southern Mississippi Valley. Behind it, a weak trough settles into the eastern United States and briefly turns our flow more northwesterly. A front accompanies that change September 8 to 10. We will have noticeably cooler weather after that front. The eastern trough erodes later in week two. The rest of the month features a more neutral westerly flow: no strong ridge, no deep trough, no cold intrusions. Temperatures step down gradually toward typical September weather. With the normal temperatures themselves falling nine to ten degrees over the month, September 2026 will feel like a bigger transition month than usual. Precipitation makes the sharper break. July and August both ran wet; September looks drier than average. Tropical activity is the wildcard — September is the heart of a hurricane season inhibited overall by El Niño. Impact from a tropical system here is not expected, but it is not impossible. September Outlook at a Glance |Week|Temperature|Precipitation| |-|-|-| |Week 1 (September 1–7)|Well above average|Below average| |Week 2 (September 8–14)|Near average|Slightly below average| |Week 3 (September 15–21)|Slightly above average|Slightly below average| |Week 4 (September 22–30)|Near average|Slightly below average| |Overall for September|Above average|Slightly below average| Other Items of Note Here are the data sources influencing our September forecast: Three long-range models (from the ECMWF, CMC, and GFS). During the three days in which this forecast was developed, the models went from widely divergent individual predictions for September to good agreement on this warm/dry scenario. We chose the ECMWF for the forecast graphic since it looked the most reasonable across the Southeast. Teleconnections, or large-scale links in atmospheric pressure and climate anomalies: North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), Arctic Oscillation (AO), Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), Pacific-North American pattern (PNA). All of these tend to have weak correlations to our weather this time of year, but all were particularly weak signals and unhelpful this year. The currently strong and strengthening El Niño also has weak correlations to our weather this time of year (except to weaken tropical system development). But because it is about to become a major player in our weather, it will get its own section for discussion below. As always, this forecast is built from scratch. We work from the data to reach our own conclusions, then check the NOAA Climate Prediction Center outlook for comparison. This month our conclusions are close to the NOAA September Outlook. The warmest water still hugs the coast of South America. The warmth tapers westward toward the central Pacific. That east-loaded shape is the classic form of El Niño. That classic shape matters for winter: events with heat concentrated in the eastern Pacific produce the most reliable response over North America, strengthening the subtropical jet and steering storms along the Gulf Coast and up the East Coast — creating opportunities for strong winter storms in the Southern Appalachians. The graphic below shows Sea Surface Temperature anomalies across the globe; note the equatorial Pacific—that’s a strong El Niño in progress. Last month we said this would be a very strong El Niño. It will be — and it has the potential to become the strongest on record. The event peaks in late fall, holds through early winter before gradually fading in late winter and spring. (See the graphic below showing model guidance for when El Niño will peak.) The strongest El Niños since 1950 (when detailed records began) were in 1982-83, 1997-98, and 2015-16. Forecasts at this point in their development tend to overshoot peaks, so we say potential rather than certainty for the record. “Very strong” is not in doubt. For the season ahead, the outline has not changed. Strong, east-based El Niño winters in the Southern Appalachians run wetter than normal, with an active southern storm track delivering more systems than an average year. The winter looks to have stronger and more frequent storms; some of these may produce significant snow in the mountains. However, the same system that gives Beech, Sugar, and Bald Mountains and Mt Mitchell over a foot can give the Foothills just a cold rain. That does not mean the Foothills escape snow and ice; it means precipitation type will be the hard call. We will have much more to say in the RaysWeather.com Fearless Forecast for Winter 2026-27, published the third week of October. Although not directly related to the El Niño, another ocean anomaly is fading in the Atlantic with potential impact on our weather. The cool patch in the Gulf of Guinea (off the coast of West Africa) is called an Atlantic Niña. It has faded to something barely detectable, so El Niño's wind shear now stands alone as the main brake on the Atlantic hurricane season. The rest of the world's oceans remain unusually warm — the background that gives us warmer nights and heavier downpours when rain does come.
